# Getting Started

## Setup Instructions

The Pico needs to be connected to your computer through the USB cable for power (unless provided externally), to upload a program on it, and to communicate with it during the execution of the program (printing in a terminal or reading user input from keyboard).

### First binaries

Binaries are files that contain machine instructions for the Pico. The file extension is `.uf2`. When programming in C, such a binary is produced on your computer and needs to be transferred to the Pico. When using micropython, the micropython interpreter is the binary that needs to be transferred to the Pico. After this, python programs can be transferred to it to be interpreted on the machine.

Here, we will follow the [Your First Binaries](https://github.com/raspberrypi/documentation/blob/master/documentation/asciidoc/microcontrollers/c_sdk/your_first_binary.adoc#your-first-binaries) section of the Pico tutorial to practice this step and test the Pico.

To load a program on the Pico, follow this process:

  * Starting from a board disconnected from the computer, press the BOOTSEL button and insert the USB connection to your computer at the same time.
  * The Pico should show up as a USB drive on your computer.
  * Copy the executable `.uf2` file on this drive.
  * This should upload the program on the Pico and restart it automatically.

### LED Blink

Download and install the [Blink UF2](https://github.com/raspberrypi/pico-sdk-prebuilts/releases/latest/download/blink_universal.uf2) file. This file supports all Pico variants.
If all goes well, you should see the integrated LED blink on your board.

### USB Serial communication

Download and install the ['Hello World' UF2](https://github.com/raspberrypi/pico-sdk-prebuilts/releases/latest/download/hello_universal.uf2) file. This file should also support all Pico variants.
Once it is installed and running, open a Serial monitor and connect it to the port of the board.
The default baud rate is 115200.

### Programming environment

We recommend using Visual Studio Code for this project, both for C/C++ programming and for MicroPython.

There are extensions available that greatly facilitate the development of programs. These can normally be installed directly from the VS Code environment.

* [Pico-vscode](https://github.com/raspberrypi/pico-vscode)
* [MicroPico](https://github.com/paulober/MicroPico)

### Example project

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## C

Go ahead and start a new project from an example. On VS Code, click on the Pico icon, on the left pane. Click new C/C++ project from example. Select your architecture (e.g. Pico 2 W) and an example, for instance blink. Select the folder where it will save the files, and create the new project. If VS Code tells you that you are in restricted mode, click manage and select "in trusted folder". Select the .c file and inspect it. Then click again on the Pico icon and click compile project. This will create an executable `.uf2` file in the `build` subfolder. Upload that file to the Pico to test the program.


## MicroPython

First, you need to download and install the version of MicroPython for your device at the following [documentation page](https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/microcontrollers/micropython.html#drag-and-drop-micropython).
This is a `uf2` file that needs to be uploaded as usual to the Pico.

In VS Code, click on the Pico icon on the left pane. Select new micropython project. Give a name to the project, select a location for the folder, and create the project. If VS Code tells you that you are in restricted mode, click manage and select "in trusted folder". Open the `.py` file and inspect the code. Right click on the source file on the explorer and select run current file on Pico to try it.


:::
